newsitem.title: UK: Britain considers dropping rabies law.
newsitem.headline: Britain considers dropping rabies law.

text.p: Britain's agriculture minister is planning to propose dropping the country's controversial quarantine laws, regarded as the world's toughest rabies controls, The Times newspaper said on Monday.
Instead Douglas Hogg is suggesting strict new rules on vaccination and blood testing and a passport-for-pets scheme based on the Swedish system.

"The move follows intense pressure on the government from groups, including diplomats and service families, who claim that British policy, enforced since 1901, is too draconian and out of proportion to the threat," the newspaper said.

Under Britain's anti-rabies system thousands of family pets face six months quarantined in kennels each year. They are confined in prison-like pens and not allowed to roam freely with other animals. The costs for the animal's owners, who are allowed to visits their pets, can be up to two thousand pounds ($3,150).

Under the proposals the quarantine would be dropped for European Union countries and rabies-free islands such as Cyprus and Malta. The change may also be done gradually, perhaps by shortening the quarantine time from six to about two or three months.
The proposal was circulated to cabinet ministers last month and coincided with public criticism of the law by Danish diplomat Henrik Sorensen, whose dog died in quarantine.
"Mr Hogg's action was not connected with the diplomat, but the events were simultaneous," The Times quoted a government source as saying. ($1=.6350 Pound)
